title: The route was staged
observation: Herodotus lists six regional segments totaling 111 stages and 450 parasangs between Sardis and Susa.
interpretation: The road was intelligible as a chain of serviced intervals, crossings, defiles, forts, and resting places.
limits: The itinerary is a Greek literary report, not a surviving Persian road survey; parasangs are not converted to kilometres and the six segments are not coordinates.

title: An ordinary journey remained long
observation: Herodotus gives ninety days for Sardis to Susa after stating a rate of 150 stades per day.
interpretation: Road infrastructure made a long journey supportable; it did not abolish distance for people, baggage, or armies.
limits: The ninety-day calculation belongs to Herodotus's own itinerary arithmetic and is not a measured average, minimum, caravan schedule, army march, or all-season travel time.

title: The message changed carriers
observation: Herodotus describes one horse and rider for each day's stage, passing a dispatch onward through weather, darkness, and successive handoffs.
interpretation: The relay compressed message time by replacing exhausted carriers rather than making one traveler move impossibly fast.
limits: Herodotus 8.98 gives the operating principle but no Sardis–Susa duration; later seven-day claims remain a different source and are not plotted here.

title: Stations provisioned real travelers
observation: Persepolis Fortification records document food issued to travelers and messengers, vouchers made at road stations, and journeys involving lands from Media to India and Bactria.
interpretation: The relay system required stores, authorizations, accounting, and local personnel—an administrative network beneath the famous riders.
limits: The archive is a surviving regional fragment centred on Persis and Elam, not a complete empire-wide postal ledger or a count of every station, traveler, ration, or route.
